Judgment:
1.

The present is a complaint filed under section 16 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954
(Pfa Act), alleging that the accused persons have violated the provisions of the Pfa Act and Rules

. 
The accused no. 1 is stated to be the vendor-cum-proprietor of M/s Raju Bhati Store, from where the food article, that is, 'Dal Arhar' was lifted for sampling.

Accused no. 2 is stated to be the proprietor of M/s. Ram Bhagat Prem Chand who had allegedly supplied the said food article to the vendor accused no. 1.
2.

As per the complaint, on 16.11.2005, food officials consisting of Food Inspector (FI) Gian Chand and Food Assistant (FA) J. P. Bhardwaj under the supervision of Local Health Authority (LHA)/SDM Sh. Yogesh Pratap reached along with their staff at the shop of accused no. 1 at Gali No.
10, Main Road, Gopalpur, PO Azad Pur, Delhi - 09 where the accused no. 1 was found conducting the business of various food articles, which were lying stored for sale for human consumption.
The FI disclosed his identity and expressed his intention to purchase a sample of Dal Arhar from the vendor lying in open wooden box (ready for sale) bearing no label declaration, to which he agreed.

1
The sample was then lifted as per procedure prescribed under the PFA Act and Rules.
Each sample was separately packed, fastened, marked and sealed and necessary documents were prepared at the spot, including the Notice as per Form-VI, panchnama, etc.
The price of sample was paid to the vendor.
Thereafter, one counterpart of the sample was sent to the Public Analyst (PA) in intact condition and the other two counterparts were deposited with SDM/LHA.
Vide report dated 12.12.2005, the PA found the sample to be adulterated on the ground that it was coloured with synthetic colouring matter 'Tartrazine'.
Upon receipt of report, the SDM/LHA ordered investigation which was carried out by the FI.
It was disclosed by the vendor at the time of lifting the sample that he had purchased the food article from accused no. 2.
The role of accused no. 2 was ascertained and after completion of investigation, sanction under section 20 of the PFA Act was obtained from the Director PFA.

The complaint was then filed in the court by FI on 05.07.2006 against both the accused persons alleging violation of section 2(ia)(j) and (m) of PFA Act as well as Rules 23, 28 and 29 of PFA Rules, as punishable section 7/16(1A) of PFA Act.
3.
As the complaint was filed in writing by a public servant, recording of pre-summoning evidence was dispensed with and the accused persons were summoned vide order dated 05.07.2006.
The matter was then listed for pre-charge evidence, wherein the complainant examined PW-1 FI Gian Chand.

On the basis of his deposition, order on charge dated 28.07.2009 was passed and charges were framed against both the accused persons for commission of the offence punishable under section 7/16(1A) PFA Act, being violation of section 2(ia)(a), (b), (j) and (m) of PFA Act, to which they pleaded not guilty and claimed trial.

At the trial, the witness already examined in pre-charge stage was recalled for further cross-examination in post-charge stage and additionally, the prosecution examined PW-2 FA J. P. Bhardwaj and PW-3 Sh. Yogesh Pratap (SDM/LHA) in post-charge stage.

4. At the trial, PW-1, PW-2 and PW-3 who were part of the team that had visited the spot for sample proceedings, deposed about the proceedings conducted by them on 16.11.2005 and narrated the steps undertaken by them during the sample proceedings, including disclosing their identity,
expressing intention to purchase sample for analysis, lifting the sample of 1500 gms of Dal Arhar (ready for sale), thoroughly mixing it using a clean and dry jhaba, dividing them and putting in three separate clean and dry sample bottles, separately sealing, packing and marking the sample bottles,
and obtaining signatures of vendor and witnesses.

They also proved the necessary documents including the vendor's receipt Ex. PW-1/A, Notice as per Form-VI Ex. PW-1/B, Panchnama Ex.
PW-1/C and Notice under section 14-A PFA Act Ex. PW-1/D.
Statement of the vendor Ex. PW-1/E
was recorded.

On the next working day, that is 17.11.2005, one counterpart of sample along with Memo as per Form-VII were sent to PA for analysis vide PA Receipt Ex. PW-1/F and remaining two counterparts with copy of Memos were deposited with LHA/SDM vide receipt Ex. PW-1/G.
PA report Ex. PW-1/H was received and upon direction of SDM/LHA, further investigation was carried out by PW-1.
He sent letter Ex. PW-1/I to the STO and obtained its reply.
He sent letter Ex. PW-1/J to the accused no. 1 and received his reply Ex. PW-1/K.
He sent letter Ex. PW-1/L and reminder Ex.
PW-1/M to accused no. 2 which was replied vide letter Ex. PW-1/N wherein he disowned the sale of sampled commodity.
Another letter Ex. PW-1/O and reminder Ex. PW- 1/O1 were written to accused no. 2 which was replied vide Ex. PW-1/P.

Letters Ex. PW-1/Q and Ex. PW-1/R were written to STO who gave replies including Ex. PW-1/R1 wherein it was informed that after dissolution of the In Re vs A-1) Raj Kumar on 17 November, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/86593070/
2 partnership firm, accused no. 2 Mangat Rai was the sole proprietor of M/s. Ram Bhagat Prem Chand.

sentences.text: After conclusion of investigation, sanction Ex. PW-1/S was taken from the Director PFA and the complaint Ex. PW-1/T was filed in the court.
After this, intimation letter Ex. PW-1/U with copy of PA report was sent to the accused persons through registered post vide postal receipt Ex. PW-1/V.
The witnesses were duly cross-examined by Ld.

Defence counsel for both the accused persons wherein they denied that the sample proceedings were not proper or that the bottles were not clean and dry or that the test adopted by the PA was not a sure test.
5. Statements of the accused persons under section 313 CrPC were recorded on 01.05.2012 wherein they denied the allegations and pleaded innocence.

Accused no. 1 accepted the proceedings dated 16.11.2005, though claimed that the SDM remained seated outside the shop, that no efforts were made to join public witnesses, that the FI had not cleaned the jhaba which had already been used by him to lift Haldi sold to a customer.

He took stand that he had purchased the food article from M/s.
Ram Bhagat Prem Chand vide bill no. 58607 dated 03.11.2005 and bill no. 57945 dated 26.07.2005 (the originals of which were claimed to have been misplaced for which the matter was reported to PS Mukherjee Nagar) and that the commodity had been sold by him in the same condition as purchased.
He however accepted that intimation letter with copy of PA Report was sent to him.
On the other hand, accused no. 2 expressed ignorance about the sample proceedings on the ground that he was not present at the spot.
He claimed that he had sold the Dal in sealed packets and stated that he could not say that the sample taken by the FI belonged to him.
He also claimed that no intimation letter was received by him.
The accused persons initially chose to lead defence evidence but vide order dated 23.07.2012, it was informed that no DE was to be led, upon which the matter was listed for final arguments.

Subsequently, two applications under section 311 CrPC and under section 315 CrPC were moved by the accused no. 1, which were allowed vide order dated 12.11.2013 and the accused was allowed to lead DE.
After taking a number of adjournments thereafter, it was again informed on 19.01.2016 that no DE was to be led.
Thus, there is no evidence led by any of the accused persons in defence.

6. It is in these circumstances, Ld. SPP for the complainant has argued that the complainant has been able to establish its case against the accused persons beyond reasonable doubt, on the ground that the accused persons have not been able to rebut the findings in the PA report dated 12.12.2005.
It is pointed out that the accused persons have failed to exercise their right under section 13(2) PFA Act and failed to get the sample analysed from Central Food Laboratory (CFL).
It is submitted that all the witnesses have supported its case and no major contradiction can be seen in their testimony.

7. On the other hand, the respective Ld. Defence Counsel for the accused persons have submitted that the sample proceedings were not conducted properly and that there are various missing links in the testimony of witnesses.
It is submitted that the PA report and intimation letter were never served upon the accused persons and they were prevented from exercising their right under section 13(2) PFA Act.
It is pointed out that no AD Card or proof of service has been placed in record by the complainant.

Ld. Counsel have then contended that no percentage or extent of synthetic colour Tartrazine has been mentioned in the report of the chemical expert and it might be possible that only traces of colour were present.

Relying upon the judgement of Maya Ram v. State of Punjab [1987(II) PFA Cases 320], it is contended that paper chromatography test used by the PA for In Re vs A-1) Raj Kumar on 17 November, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/86593070/
3 detecting food colours is not a sure test and thus, the report of PA becomes unreliable.

sentences.text: The report has also been questioned on the ground that there has been an unexplained delay of twenty days in signing the report by the PA, relying upon the judgements titled as Delhi Administration v. Amar Chand [2012 (3) JCC 1930] and State of Gujrat v. Vishramdas Virumal [2005 (1) FAC 48].

sentences.text: It is further submitted that Tartrazine is not a harmful colouring matter as its use is permitted in many food articles.
Ld. Counsel have also submitted that Tartrazine is a water soluble colour and when the dal arhar is washed before cooking, the said colour gets washed away and no harm is caused to the consumer.

It is argued on behalf of accused no. 1 that he was only a retailer and not the manufacturer of the article and that he had purchased the same from accused no. 2 against a proper bill and was selling the same in the same state, thereby claiming the benefit of warranty under section 19(2) of PFA Act.

The accused no. 2 on the other hand has contended that the original bill of purchase has not been proved on record and in any case, there is nothing to show that he Dal in question had been supplied by him because when lifted, the Dal was lying in loose condition in a wooden box bearing no label declaration.
It is finally contended that the laboratory in which the sample was analysed and the testing method were not notified under the Rules and therefore the prosecution is bad in law.
8. I have heard the arguments advanced by Ld. SPP for the complainant and the respective Ld.
Defence Counsel for both the accused persons
and have carefully perused the material available on record.

9. It is to be understood that the charge framed against the accused persons is for violation of section 2(ia)(a), (b), (j) and (m) of the PFA Act read with Rules 23, 28 & 29 of PFA Rules with respect to 'adulteration'.

Under section 2(ia)(a) of PFA Act, the prosecution has to establish that the purchaser had demanded a food article of a specific nature, substance or quality and the article sold was, to his prejudice, either not of the nature, substance or quality demanded, or was not of the nature, substance or quality which it purported or represented to be.
Under section 2(ia)(b) of PFA Act, it has to be established that the food article contained any substance affecting injuriously the nature, substance or quality thereof.
Section 2(ia)(j) specifically deals with colouring matter which is present other than prescribed or is present beyond the prescribed limits of variability.

Section 2(ia)(m) of PFA Act deals with situation where the quality or purity of an article falls below the prescribed standard or its constituents are present in quantities not within the prescribed limits of variability.
10. The court is required to ascertain if the offence of selling an adulterated food article has been proved and if so, which of the accused persons would be liable for the offence.
11. To begin with, it is seen that the accused persons have not exercised their right under section 13(2) PFA Act for getting the sample analysed through CFL.

For this, the arguments are that PA report with intimation letter were never served upon them (though in his statement under section 313 CrPC, accused no. 1 admitted the factum of sending the intimation letter to him, as correct).
12.

As per the scheme of the Act, under section 13(2) of the Act, after institution of prosecution against the accused, the LHA is required to forward a copy of the PA report to the accused,
In Re vs A-1) Raj Kumar on 17 November, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/86593070/
4 informing that he may apply to the Court, within 10 days of receipt of report, for getting the sample (second counterpart) analysed by CFL.
Thus, this provision mandates sending of PA report to the accused by the LHA, after filing of the complaint.

It is a settled law that if the report is not so sent, it would cause prejudice to the accused and would be fatal to the prosecution because this right cannot be allowed to be frustrated by the prosecution.

However, if the accused himself forgoes his right,
then he cannot say that he was prejudiced.
13. At the outset, there is no merit in the contention that the PA report was not received by the accused persons, and particularly by the accused no. 1.

PW-1 and PW-3 both deposed about sending the copy of PA report with intimation letter Ex. PW-1/U through registered post vide receipt Ex.
PW-1/V.
The office file containing the documents had been produced at the time of evidence of PW-1 (though objected by the ld. Defence counsel for want of original).

It is to be seen that despite taking an objection (it is not clear as to which of the two accused persons had taken the objection),
the correctness of this record has not been rebutted or questioned by the defence.

Not even a single suggestion was given to these witnesses that the postal receipt Ex. PW-1/V was a forged or fabricated document or that no such letter was sent or that it was sent at an incorrect address.

For that matter, it is revealed that in his statement under section 313 CrPC, it is only the accused no. 2 who has denied sending of the letter to him and the accused no. 1 has accepted this fact as correct.
Thus, as far as accused no. 1 is concerned, he cannot take benefit on this count.
14. Once this fact is so established, section 27 of the General Clauses Act would come into play.
It is not the case of the accused persons that the said letter Ex. PW-1/U was sent at incorrect addresses.
No such stand has been taken by the accused persons at any stage of trial including prosecution evidence, statement of accused or defence evidence.

In such a position, when a letter had been sent through registered post at a correct and proper address, there would be a presumption of service under section 27 of the General Clauses Act in favour of the complainant.

The burden would not upon be the complainant to show delivery of the letter and such burden would now shift upon the accused persons to show that the letter was not so delivered despite having been sent at correct addresses through registered post.
But the accused persons have not led any evidence to this effect.
No attempt was made by them to summon the records of postal department to show as to whom the letters were delivered or if they remained undelivered.
There is no evidence to show that the letters were not delivered to the accused persons.
Accused persons have not claimed that they were not staying at those addresses or were staying at some other addresses or that the letters could not have been served upon them at the relevant time.
It is not their claim that they were not available at the said addresses or had shifted from those addresses.
Thus, accused persons have failed to rebut the presumption under section 27 of the General Clauses Act.
As PW-1 and PW-3 deposed that the registered letters were not received back undelivered, the burden would be upon the accused persons to prove anything to the contrary.
By not leading any evidence to support their stand, the version of the accused persons remains unsubstantiated.
Therefore, it has to be held that the intimation letter and PA report were delivered upon the accused persons in due course.
The accused persons cannot therefore opt to simply deny the things and claim that PA report was not received by them.
The accused no. 1 particularly cannot deny the same when he has admitted that the letter was sent to him.

In Re vs A-1) Raj Kumar on 17 November, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/86593070/
5 15.
This is not one of the cases where the accused persons were prevented from exercising their right under section 13(2) of PFA Act.
The accused persons have deliberately and voluntarily forgiven their right under section 13(2) of the Act.
It is not a case where the right of the accused persons got frustrated due to any delay in filing the prosecution.
The nature of synthetic colours is such that no period of delay would change its nature, quality or quantity.
Such argument is liable to be rejected.
16. The commodity in the present case is Dal Arhar (split pulse) which is food grain and has to be tested as per the standards prescribed for food grains.
The article falls in Item A.18.06.09 of Appendix B to the PFA Rules.
17. The present case is based on the findings of PA as given in report Ex. PW-1/H that has found the presence of the synthetic colouring matter Tartrazine in the sample analysed.
There is nothing for the court to disbelieve the PA report wherein artificial synthetic colour tartrazine has been detected in the food article.
Report of chemical expert is admissible in evidence under section 293 CrPC without formal examination of such expert.

As far as this report is concerned, the contents and findings therein have not been disputed by the defence, though it is claimed that such findings are wrong on account of incorrect sampling methodology.
It is nowhere the defence of the accused persons that there was some mistake in the report (though it is claimed that the method of analysis adopted by PA was not a sure and reliable test).
The accused persons never applied to cross-examine the PA when this option was available to them under section 293 CrPC, so as to question her on her report or to seek any clarification.

It is not the defence of the accused persons that no colour was detected, or was detected wrongly, or that any such colour was a result of natural environment or the food article having been exposed to natural environment.
No suggestion to this effect was given to any witness during cross-examination.

No such defence was raised by the accused persons in their statement under section 313 CrPC.
18.
Rather the accused persons have taken contradictory stands in their defence.

As far as accused no. 1 is concerned, he took a stand at the trial that some Tartrazine color was already there in the sample bottles (as suggested to PW-1 and PW-3) but in his statement under section 313 CrPC, he never took such a defence but claimed that the jhaba used for lifting the sample was not clean and dry and it had already been used for lifting Haldi which was sold to another customer (which stand was never taken during the cross examination of PWs).
Even the accused no. 2 suggested to PW-3 that the paper envelope used had some yellow material in it (though this stand was never taken by accused no. 2 in his statement under section 313 CrPC).
Interestingly, by taking such a stand, the accused persons, accused no. 1 in particular, has lost the right to take a contradictory plea that no colour was there in the sample.

It is apparent that atleast the accused no. 1 has accepted the presence of colour in the sample, though has claimed that it was on account of wrong sampling procedure and due to alleged presence of Tartrazine in the sample bottles.
Thus even from this angle, it is evident that the sample was having food colour tartrazine.
19. As per Rule 23 of PFA Rules, addition of a colouring matter to any article of food except as specifically permitted by the Rules is prohibited.
Rule 28 provides the details of colours permitted for use and Rule 29 enlists the food in which synthetic colours are permitted.

A bare perusal of this list would show that it does not mention food grains as the food in which any such synthetic colour In Re vs A-1) Raj Kumar on 17 November, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/86593070/
6 is permitted.
The obvious inference is that use of such synthetic food colour is totally prohibited for use in food grains, though they are permitted in specified food articles within the prescribed limits.
Thus, there is no force in the stand of the accused persons that this colour is permitted for use in other food articles.
When the use of any such colour is absolutely prohibited for this product, no such colour can be used.

Reliance can be safely placed on the precedent titled as Delhi Administration v. Ashwani Kumar [Crl. A. 538/2013, Delhi High Court, dated 09.05.2013].
20.

entities.text: Delhi Administration v. Ashwani Kumar [Crl. A. 538/2013, Delhi High Court
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Having said so, it is immaterial to go into the question as to what was the percentage or quantity of colour used in the sample of dal arhar.
It would not make any difference if the analyst has not given the percentage of colour used.
Even if the said quantity was in traces, as being contended by the Ld. Defence Counsel, that would still make out the offence as this colour is not permitted within any limits for use in food grains.
Giving of percentage of colour would be necessary only in those samples where such colours are permitted up to certain prescribed limits and not where it is totally prohibited.
In any case, it would be for the accused persons to show as to on what basis they claim presence of such colouring matter in traces in food article in question.
The burden would be upon them to show how even traces of colour could have entered the food article being sold by them.
But no evidence has been led by the accused persons to establish this fact.
21. Again, there is no merit in the contention that Tartrazine is a water soluble colour and no prejudice would be caused to any customer because dal arhar would be washed before preparation.
As per section 19(1) of PFA Act, it shall be no defence that the food article sold had not caused any prejudice to the purchaser.

Just because some synthetic colour is water soluble and the food article is generally washed before being cooked, that gives no right to anyone to use prohibited synthetic colours in food articles in violation of statutory provisions.
Thus, it is clear that the food article dal arhar was adulterated within the meaning of section 2(ia) of PFA Act being in violation of Rule 23 read with Rules 28 and 29.

Reliance can be again placed on the precedents titled as Delhi Administration v. Ashwani Kumar [Crl. A. 538/2013, Delhi High Court, dated 09.05.2013] and Delhi Administration v. Manohar Lal [Crl. A. 153/2013, Delhi High Court, dated 18.02.2013] which are squarely applicable to this case.
22.

sentences.text: There is nothing to show that paper chromatography test is not a sure or reliable test to detect colour in food articles.
This test is internationally recognised and accepted method to detect presence of colours in food articles.
No attempt was made by the accused to apply and cross-examine the PA as to the validity and intricacies of the method adopted by her.
She would have been the best person to explain the things as she had analysed the sample.
And not only the PA, the accused persons also chose not to examine any expert witness in defence to establish their stand that the paper chromatography test is not a sure test.

The natural colours are separated and get fade away in such test and it cannot be said that natural colours cannot be differentiated from synthetic colour by adopting such test, as argued by Ld. Defence counsel.
In any case, if the accused persons were having any doubt, they should have examined chemical expert by exercising their right at appropriate stage.

In Re vs A-1) Raj Kumar on 17 November, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/86593070/
7 23.
The judgements in Maya Ram v. State of Punjab (supra) and Daulat Ram v. State of Punjab [1979(II) PFA Cases 202], as relied upon by the defence, are clearly distinguishable on facts of this case.

entities.text: Maya Ram v. State of Punjab
entities.label: PRECEDENT

entities.text: Daulat Ram v. State of Punjab [1979(II) PFA Cases 202]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: These judgements would apply only to those cases where some synthetic food colour is permitted to be used in a food article (like sweets) and the court has to determine if the synthetic colour found in the sample was permitted or unpermitted.
In such a position, the Hon'ble Court had observed that paper chromatography test would not be sufficient to find if the colour detected was permissible or not.
But these judgements would not apply to those cases where use of such colours is absolutely prohibited and not permitted for use to any extent.

Where the court need not go into the question if the colour detected was permissible or not, but has only to determine if any such colour was detected (as all such colours are prohibited), these judgements would not apply.
24. All the PWs have corroborated the stand of each other on facts.
All deposed about attempt made to join public persons as witnesses.
All deposed about steps taken during sample proceedings.
There is no contradiction in their statements that can be said to be material enough so as to go to the root of the matter.
There is nothing to disbelieve them or to shake their credibility.
It is not a case of non-compliance of any Rule or procedure.
Rather the witnesses categorically deposed about compliance of due procedure and there is nothing in their cross-examination so as to attach any falsity to their version.
All the three witnesses deposed about use of clean and dry jhaba and bottles.
PW-1 and PW-3 reiterated this fact even during their cross-examination.
Both of them categorically denied that the jhaba or bottles were not clean and dry or that some tartrazine colour was already there in the sample bottles.
As against this, there is no evidence in the form of testimony of any witness that any implement / utensil / instrument was not clean and dry.
Such suggestions given to the PWs have remained bald averments without any evidentiary support.
25. All the witnesses have corroborated the testimony of each other on material counts and there is no contradiction in their version.
All these witnesses have withstood the test of cross-examination.
All the three witnesses deposed that the food article was lying in loose condition in an open wooden box.
PW-1 deposed that they reached at the spot around 03:15 PM and PW-3 stated that they reached around 03:30 PM which is not a huge difference so as to doubt their version.
PW-1 stated that about 10 to 12 wooden boxes were there in total and PW-2 confirmed it by stating that around 8 to 10 boxes were there.
Both PW-1 and PW-2 stated that there was no Haldi or Mirch powder in any of the said boxes.
When asked, PW-1 stated that the food article was weighed in a brown paper envelope and this fact was confirmed even by PW-3.
PW-2 also deposed that the food article had been weighed, though he was never asked about the container in which it was weighed.
Both PW-1 and PW-2 deposed that two customers had been requested to join the proceedings but they did not agree.
26. The fate of the case depends on quality of witnesses and not their quantity or designation or professions.
There is no rule of law that requires the evidence of food officials to be viewed with any suspicion.
What is required is that attempt is made to join public persons as witnesses as a matter of prudence.
The court is not oblivious of reluctance of public persons to join such legal proceedings that involves lengthy procedural formalities and strict future commitments.
But non joining of such witnesses would not negate the testimony of official witnesses when they are otherwise truthful and credit worthy and have withstood the test of cross-examination.
No motive has shown to exist giving

In Re vs A-1) Raj Kumar on 17 November, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/86593070/
8 them reason to depose falsely against the accused persons.

The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Shriram Labhaya v. MCD [1948-1997 FAC (SC) 483] has categorically held that testimony of the Food Inspector alone, if believed, is sufficient to convict the accused and there is no requirement of independent corroboration by public persons unless the testimony suffers from fatal inconsistencies.
No such inconsistency can be seen in this case.
No violation of any rule or provision has been pointed out by the defence.
27. Further, there is no merit in the stand of the accused persons that the report of PA is not reliable on the ground that the same was signed after a few days.
As per the report, the sample was analysed from 22.11.2005 to 22.11.2005 (showing that analysis was completed on the same day, which is quite improbable).
The report was signed on 12.12.2005, that is, after about twenty days.
Well, the court is not in a position to term such a period as "unexplained delay" particularly when no opportunity was granted to the PA to explain any such delay.
As already stated, the accused persons did not exercise their option to apply and cross examine the PA under section 293 CrPC.
She would have been the best person to explain any such delay.
Such delay could be due to any reason including vacations, leaves, administrative reasons, official exigencies, analytical studies or even typographical error etc.
But when no opportunity has been given to the PA, the court cannot on hypothetical assumptions assume that the said delay has not been explained so as to negate the entire prosecution case.
No clarification on this point was sought even from the FI who had conducted the investigation.
Thus, no benefit can be given to the accused persons on this count.
28. Moving ahead, the defence claims that method of analysis and laboratories were not specified by the Rule-making authority and thus, prosecution was bad.
It has been argued that the prosecution was launched on 05.07.2006 on the basis of the Public Analyst's report dated 12.12.2005.
Relying upon the judgement of the Hon'ble Supreme Court titled Pepsico India Holdings Pvt. Ltd. v. Food Inspector [2010(2) PFA Cases 310], the Ld.

sentences.text:
Defence counsel have argued that the prosecution was bad in law and no prosecution could have been launched because Section 23, which empowered the Central Government to make rules to carry out the provisions of the Act, was amended with effect from 01.04.1976 and Sub Clause (ee) and (hh) were inserted in Clause (1A) of section 23 which included power to define/ designate laboratories competent to analyze the sample as well as define the methods of analysis to be used.
29.

Well, if such an interpretation is to be given, then all the cases of whatever nature, of whatever ingredient and of any amount of adulteration, registered after 01.04.1976 would lead to outright dismissal en block, without going into any other evidence, on the ground that laboratories or methods have not been specified, and particularly between 01.04.1976 and 25.03.2008 on the ground that method of analysis was not specified.
But such an interpretation is not possible or plausible.

There are large number of precedents during this period where the guilty persons had been booked and convicted and their convictions and sentences upheld by the superior courts throughout the country.

30. As far as analysis by the PA and launching of the prosecution on her report is concerned, it is to be seen that as per the scheme of the Act the first analysis of the sample/food product is done by the Public Analyst in terms of section 8, 11 and 13 of the Act.

The Public Analyst is appointed by the In Re vs A-1) Raj Kumar on 17 November, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/86593070/
9 Central or State government by way of notification in the official gazette.

sentences.text: Unless the report of Public Analyst is superseded by that of Director, CFL, this report holds good for all purposes and remains effective and valid and can be used as evidence of the facts stated therein.
There is nothing to show that the PA Smt. Mohini Srivastava was not validly appointed as Public Analyst or could not have analyzed the sample.
Such stand taken at the trial was never proved and PA was not sought to be cross-examined under section 293 CrPC to explain the facts.
Even her report also mentions that she had been duly appointed.
31. At this stage it would be worthwhile to highlight extracts of Preface to the first edition of the DGHS Manual.

The same reads as:
"The Prevention of Food Adulteration Act 1954 came into effect from Ist June 1955.
Adulteration has been defined in section 2 of the PFA Act.

Under sub-clause (I) of clause (i) of section 2, it has been stated that an article of food shall be deemed to be adulterated, if the quality or purity of the article falls below the prescribed standards or its constituents are present in quantities which are in excess of the prescribed limits of variability.
The specifications prescribed for the purity of various articles of food have been given in Appendix 'B' of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules.

The analysts as well as food technologists and Analysts employed in various organisations have been using various method of tests for the determination of different components whose limits have been laid down under these rules.
As the methods adopted by Analysts are different, the results obtained may sometime differ even in the case of the same food product analysed at different food laboratories.

The Central Committee for Food Standards considered this subject in detail and desired that methods of tests as available with the various institutions like Indian Standards Institution, Directorate of Marketing and Inspection etc. be aligned and published for the guidance of Public Analysts and other analytical chemists so as to have a uniformity in the reports.

A sub- committee under the convenership of Dr. Sadgopal,
Deputy Director General Indian Standards Institution with Shri R.K. Malik, Senior Marketing Officer, Directorate of Marketing and Inspection and Shri S.N. Mitra,
Director, Central Food Laboratory, Calcutta was constituted for the purpose.
These methods of tests having been recommended by the Sub-committee and approved by Central Committee for Food Standards
are published for the guidance of all concerned."
32. This Manual was published in the year 1975 and its chief purpose was to lay down the methods to be employed for analysis of different food products.
As is evident from its Preface the Central Committee for Food Standards published the same so as to be the guidance for Public Analysts and Analytical Chemists to have a uniformity in the reports.

Section 3 of the PFA Act empowers the Central Government to form/constitute the above Committee, that is, Central Committee for Food Standards to advise the Central as well as the State Governments on matters arising out of administration of this Act and to carry out the other functions assigned to it under this Act.

In Re vs A-1) Raj Kumar on 17 November, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/86593070/
10 33.
Therefore, on the day of analysis of the sample in question, the Public Analyst was competent to analyze the sample and use the method she deemed fit for the purpose of analysis of the sample.

There is nothing to show that any method adopted by her was not a sure or reliable test, particularly when she was not even sought to be cross-examined by applying under section 293 CrPC on this point.
34. As far as Pepsico's case (supra) is concerned, the judgement cannot be read in isolation or selectively.
It has to be read as a whole keeping in mind the purpose and the scheme of the Act which intends to safeguard the public at large from the evil/ menace of food adulteration.

The relevant portion of the judgement relied upon by the Ld. Defence counsel reads as:
"34.

As far as Grounds 1 and 2 are concerned, the High Court was not convinced with the submission made on behalf of the appellants that in the absence of any prescribed and validated method of analysis under Section 23(1-A)(ee) and (hh) of the 1954 Act,
the report of the Public Analyst, who had used the DGHS method, could not be relied upon, especially when even the Laboratories, where the test for detection of insecticides and pesticides in an article of food could be undertaken, had not been specified.

The observation of the Division Bench of the High Court that if the submissions made on behalf of the Appellants herein were to be accepted, the mechanism of the Act and the Rules framed thereunder would come to a grinding halt, is not acceptable to us, since the same could lead to a pick and choose method to suit the prosecution.

However, in any event, the percentage of Carbofuran detected in the sample of Pepsico which was sent for examination to the Forensic Laboratory is within the tolerance limits prescribed for Sweetened Carbonated Water with effect from 17th June, 2009.

35. The High Court also misconstrued the provisions of Section 23(1-A)(ee) and (hh)
in holding that the same were basically enabling provisions and were not mandatory and could, in any event, be solved by the Central Government by framing Rules thereunder, by which specified tests to be held in designated Laboratories could be spelt out.
Consequently, the High Court also erred in holding that the non- formulation of Rules under the aforesaid provisions of the 1954 Act could not be said to be fatal for the prosecution."
35. Thus, in that case, even the laboratories where the tests were to be performed for determining content of pesticides in sweetened carbonated drinks were not specified.
At that time, it was no Rule framed by the government specifying as to what quantity of pesticides was permissible.
But in the case at hand, specific Rules are there with respect to prohibition of use of artificial synthetic colours in foodgrains.
In this case, prosecution is for violation of section 2(ia)(a), (b), (j) and (m) of the Act.
The present case would be squarely covered by the judgement of the Hon'ble Supreme Court titled as Prem Ballab v. State (Delhi Administration) [(1977) 1 SCC 173].

sentences.text: This judgement was discussed even in Pepsico's case, but was never disturbed and was sought to be distinguished on the ground that this was dealing with colouring matter (as in the present case) and not with pesticides in carbonated water.

But when the present case is also with respect to colouring matter and not In Re vs A-1) Raj Kumar on 17 November, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/86593070/
11 pesticides in carbonated water, the ruling in Pepsico's case would not help the accused persons.

36. It is therefore clear that the food article in question was an adulterated food article being sold for human consumption by accused no.
1.
It is no defence available to the accused no. 1 to claim that he was not the manufacturer of the commodity in question or that he was only a retailer selling the same.
A seller or packer or distributor or manufacturer would operate in different fields and all of them can be held liable in their separate areas.
Sale of adulterated food article is prohibited.
The definition of 'sale' under section 2 (xiii) is very wide which includes storing or exposing for sale as a retailer and even attempt to sell and also sale for analysis.
There is no requirement that the sample can be lifted only when a food article is actually being sold to any customer.
Sale of commodity to the FI and also exposing for sale would be covered under the PFA Act.

The only benefit which an accused can claim on this ground is under section 19(2) of PFA Act which would apply only if he is able to show that he had purchased the product against a warranty and had been selling the product in the same manner as purchased by him.
37. In the present case, the accused no. 1 claimed that he had purchased the dal from M/s. Ram Bhagat Prem Chand.
Even on the day of sampling, he informed the FI that he has purchased the Dal from this concern and he also furnished photocopy of one invoice no. 57945 dated 26.09.2005 Mark - X.
This stand was reiterated by him in his reply Ex. PW1/K given to the FI during the course of investigation.
38. Well, the burden would only be upon the accused no. 1 to prove the necessary facts to claim the benefit of warranty under section 19(2) of PFA Act.

Though the original bill has never been produced and proved on record by the accused no. 1, yet the supplier accused no. 2 has not seriously disputed the same but has only denied the sampled commodity to be the one that was sold through this bill.
It is important to note that the accused no. 1 had claimed that the food article was the one as purchased by him through the bill no. 57945 dated 26.09.2005.

However, in this statement under section 313 CrPC, he stated about two different bills no. 58607 dated 03.11.2005 (which has never seen the light of the day nor was put to any witness) and no. 57945 dated 26.07.2005 (the date is different from Mark-X).
In any case, none of these two bills have been produced in original in court.
It appears that even the accused is not in a position to identify if the food article was purchased through bill no. 58607 or 57945 or for that matter any other bill.

There is nothing to identify the Dal lifted from the spot in open and loose condition to be a part of any Dal purchased by accused no. 1 vide any of these bills or any other bill of accused no. 2 or even from any other supplier.

The Dal lying in open wooden boxes without any label declaration could have been purchased from any supplier and in the absence of any further material, just on the oral version of the vendor and supplying of one previous bill, accused no. 2 could not have been implicated straightaway.

The material is not sufficient to show that the Dal in question was a part of the articles supplied only by accused no. 2 vide bill Mark - X.
In Re vs A-1) Raj Kumar on 17 November, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/86593070/
12 39.

It is important to note that in his statement under section 313 CrPC, accused no. 1 claimed that the original bills had been misplaced for which a complaint was also made to PS Mukherjee Nagar vide DD no. 77B dated 30.04.2012.
Despite that, no evidence was led by him to prove such record.

When the matter was at the stage of final arguments, two applications under sections 315 CrPC and 311 CrPC were moved, taking a stand that the accused no. 1 wished to prove the DD entry and his defences.
Both the applications were allowed vide detailed order dated 12.11.2013.
However, no defence witness was examined on as many as eight dates of hearing thereafter.

Then on 19.01.2016,
it was again stated by ld.
Defence counsel that no D.E was to be led.
It is not explained as to what prevented the accused no. 1 from leading defence evidence even after his applications were allowed.
40. The fact remains that neither the original bills are on record nor any DD entry showing any complaint lodged with respect to loss of such bills.
No witness from the concerned PS has been examined to establish any such complaint.

It therefore cannot be said that the bills have been misplaced from accused no. 1.
41.

The record would also show that it was necessary for the bills to be produced in court, primarily because of the stand taken by the accused during the investigation about one bill and stand taken by him in statement under section 313 CrPC about multiple bills.
Even the bill Mark - X is not free from doubt.
It mentions various food articles like Chana, Dal Chana, Moth Dhula, Urad Chilka, Malka in addition to one Dal mentioned at Sr. No. 1.
Dal Arhar is nowhere mentioned in this bill and there is some overwriting in the item mentioned at Sr. No. 1 which could have pertained to Dal Arhar.

Even the notings / warnings given at the foot of the bill would show that the seller claimed that he had no responsibility under PFA Act once the goods left his shop (though the validity of such a clause is also questionable).
Again, such a bill has to be in the prescribed format as per Rule 12-A of PFA Rules read with Form-VIA prescribed therein.
These facts were necessary to be gone into but in the absence of the original bill, the court cannot go into such details.

42. It is also seen that even as per the accused no. 1, the sample failed because of improper sample proceedings on the ground that the jhaba was not clean and dry, that the jhaba had been previously used to sell Haldi to a customer, that the sample bottles were not clean and dry, and that some tartrazine colour was already there in the sample bottles.
It thus shows that the accused no. 1 has claimed that there was no defect or adulteration in the dal in his possession.
If he claims that the colour in the Dal was due to improper sample proceedings, then there was no reason for him to claim that adulterated Dal was supplied by some other seller.
In any case, the seller has a valid defence that the Dal sold by him was not adulterated.

Even otherwise, there is nothing to connect or identify the dal as lifted in open and loose condition by the FI from accused no. 1 with any dal supplied to him by any other supplier (including the accused no. 2) in a sealed condition.

There is no evidence in the form of testimony of any witness that the dal in question was the one that was purchased by the accused no. 1 from accused no. 2, or that it was sold by him in the same state as was purchased.

The benefit of warranty under section 19(2) of the Act cannot be thus given to the accused no. 1.
43.
The case in hand would be covered under section 2(ia)(a) of PFA Act as there is evidence to show that it was not of the nature, substance or quality which it is "purported" to be as per PFA Rules.

The In Re vs A-1) Raj Kumar on 17 November, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/86593070/
13 case would fall under section 2(ia)(j) as there is presence of colour which is not permitted in this article, and under section 2(ia)(m) of PFA Act as the constituent of colour is present in quantities not within the prescribed limits, being totally prohibited.

sentences.text: However, in the absence of quantity or percentage of colour, it cannot be said that the extent of colour used was affecting injuriously its nature, substance or quality thereof so as to make out violation of section 2(ia)(b).
Violation of section 2(ia)(j) is punishable under section 16(1A) and violation of section 2(ia)(a) and (m) is punishable under section 16(i)(a) of PFA Act.

But being graver offence, conviction can be under section 16(1A) of PFA Act.
44.
Having said so, it can be said that the complainant / prosecution has been able to establish its case and prove the guilt of the accused no. 1 beyond the shadow of reasonable doubt.

It has been proved that the accused no. 1 had sold adulterated food in violation of section 2(ia)(a), (j) and (m) of PFA Act read with Rules 23, 28 and 29 of PFA Rules, and has committed the offence punishable under section 7/16(1A) of PFA Act.

On the other hand, the accused no. 2 is entitled to be given benefit of doubt as the material is not sufficient to show that the food article had been supplied by him to the vendor or that the vendor is protected under warranty.
45. Having said so, the accused No. 1 is held guilty and convicted for the offence punishable under section 7/16(1A) of the PFA Act.
Accused no. 2 is acquitted of the charges.
46. Bail bonds of accused no. 2 shall remain in force for the next six months in terms of section 437-A, CrPC.
Matter be listed for arguments on sentence qua the accused no. 1 convict.

opennyai_summary.facts: On the basis of his deposition, order on charge dated 28.07.2009 was passed and charges were framed against both the accused persons for commission of the offence punishable under section 7/16(1A) PFA Act, being violation of section 2(ia)(a), (b), (j) and (m) of PFA Act, to which they pleaded not guilty and claimed trial.
opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
It is a settled law that if the report is not so sent, it would cause prejudice to the accused and would be fatal to the prosecution because this right cannot be allowed to be frustrated by the prosecution.
Therefore, it has to be held that the intimation letter and PA report were delivered upon the accused persons in due course.
The accused persons cannot therefore opt to simply deny the things and claim that PA report was not received by them.
The accused no. 1 particularly cannot deny the same when he has admitted that the letter was sent to him.
The accused persons have deliberately and voluntarily forgiven their right under section 13(2) of the Act.
It is not a case where the right of the accused persons got frustrated due to any delay in filing the prosecution.
The nature of synthetic colours is such that no period of delay would change its nature, quality or quantity.
It is not the defence of the accused persons that no colour was detected, or was detected wrongly, or that any such colour was a result of natural environment or the food article having been exposed to natural environment.
The obvious inference is that use of such synthetic food colour is totally prohibited for use in food grains, though they are permitted in specified food articles within the prescribed limits.
Thus, there is no force in the stand of the accused persons that this colour is permitted for use in other food articles.
When the use of any such colour is absolutely prohibited for this product, no such colour can be used.
Reliance can be safely placed on the precedent titled as Delhi Administration v. Ashwani Kumar [Crl. A. 538/2013, Delhi High Court, dated 09.05.2013].
20.
Giving of percentage of colour would be necessary only in those samples where such colours are permitted up to certain prescribed limits and not where it is totally prohibited.
As per section 19(1) of PFA Act, it shall be no defence that the food article sold had not caused any prejudice to the purchaser.
Just because some synthetic colour is water soluble and the food article is generally washed before being cooked, that gives no right to anyone to use prohibited synthetic colours in food articles in violation of statutory provisions.
Thus, it is clear that the food article dal arhar was adulterated within the meaning of section 2(ia) of PFA Act being in violation of Rule 23 read with Rules 28 and 29.
Reliance can be again placed on the precedents titled as Delhi Administration v. Ashwani Kumar [Crl. A. 538/2013, Delhi High Court, dated 09.05.2013] and Delhi Administration v. Manohar Lal [Crl. A. 153/2013, Delhi High Court, dated 18.02.2013] which are squarely applicable to this case.
22.
There is nothing to show that paper chromatography test is not a sure or reliable test to detect colour in food articles.
This test is internationally recognised and accepted method to detect presence of colours in food articles.
And not only the PA, the accused persons also chose not to examine any expert witness in defence to establish their stand that the paper chromatography test is not a sure test.
The natural colours are separated and get fade away in such test and it cannot be said that natural colours cannot be differentiated from synthetic colour by adopting such test, as argued by Ld. Defence counsel.
26. The fate of the case depends on quality of witnesses and not their quantity or designation or professions.
There is no rule of law that requires the evidence of food officials to be viewed with any suspicion.
What is required is that attempt is made to join public persons as witnesses as a matter of prudence.
The court is not oblivious of reluctance of public persons to join such legal proceedings that involves lengthy procedural formalities and strict future commitments.
But non joining of such witnesses would not negate the testimony of official witnesses when they are otherwise truthful and credit worthy and have withstood the test of cross-examination.
No motive has shown to exist giving
The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Shriram Labhaya v. MCD [1948-1997 FAC (SC) 483] has categorically held that testimony of the Food Inspector alone, if believed, is sufficient to convict the accused and there is no requirement of independent corroboration by public persons unless the testimony suffers from fatal inconsistencies.
No violation of any rule or provision has been pointed out by the defence.
27. Further, there is no merit in the stand of the accused persons that the report of PA is not reliable on the ground that the same was signed after a few days.
Well, the court is not in a position to term such a period as "unexplained delay" particularly when no opportunity was granted to the PA to explain any such delay.
Such delay could be due to any reason including vacations, leaves, administrative reasons, official exigencies, analytical studies or even typographical error etc.
But when no opportunity has been given to the PA, the court cannot on hypothetical assumptions assume that the said delay has not been explained so as to negate the entire prosecution case.
Relying upon the judgement of the Hon'ble Supreme Court titled Pepsico India Holdings Pvt. Ltd. v. Food Inspector [2010(2) PFA Cases 310], the Ld.
Well, if such an interpretation is to be given, then all the cases of whatever nature, of whatever ingredient and of any amount of adulteration, registered after 01.04.1976 would lead to outright dismissal en block, without going into any other evidence, on the ground that laboratories or methods have not been specified, and particularly between 01.04.1976 and 25.03.2008 on the ground that method of analysis was not specified.
Therefore, on the day of analysis of the sample in question, the Public Analyst was competent to analyze the sample and use the method she deemed fit for the purpose of analysis of the sample.
In this case, prosecution is for violation of section 2(ia)(a), (b), (j) and (m) of the Act.
It is no defence available to the accused no. 1 to claim that he was not the manufacturer of the commodity in question or that he was only a retailer selling the same.
A seller or packer or distributor or manufacturer would operate in different fields and all of them can be held liable in their separate areas.
Sale of adulterated food article is prohibited.
The definition of 'sale' under section 2 (xiii) is very wide which includes storing or exposing for sale as a retailer and even attempt to sell and also sale for analysis.
There is no requirement that the sample can be lifted only when a food article is actually being sold to any customer.
The benefit of warranty under section 19(2) of the Act cannot be thus given to the accused no. 1.
43.
However, in the absence of quantity or percentage of colour, it cannot be said that the extent of colour used was affecting injuriously its nature, substance or quality thereof so as to make out violation of section 2(ia)(b).
Violation of section 2(ia)(j) is punishable under section 16(1A) and violation of section 2(ia)(a) and (m) is punishable under section 16(i)(a) of PFA Act.
But being graver offence, conviction can be under section 16(1A) of PFA Act.
44.
It has been proved that the accused no. 1 had sold adulterated food in violation of section 2(ia)(a), (j) and (m) of PFA Act read with Rules 23, 28 and 29 of PFA Rules, and has committed the offence punishable under section 7/16(1A) of PFA Act.
